Meet the Polyvagal Current

The Polyvagal Current is a Polyvagal-informed model showing primary and mixed states as well as the influence of safety on the entire system.

It shows the three autonomic states as a fluid current rather than a fixed position: three circles in an infinity shape and a Safety Influence slider.

This page introduces the model. The next page in the series, How to read your own nervous system, teaches the literacy practice: how to actually use the Current with yourself. The third, The three stuck states, goes deep on what stuckness looks like in each branch.

The figure 8

The infinite current

The triple-looped figure 8 is the primary difference between this model and others; the heart of the Polyvagal Current.

This current represents autonomic regulation, flowing through each of the Polyvagal primary states. It never ends, always seeking homeostasis.

Each state and mixed state is represented dynamically as an increase or decrease in activity of the flow, which condenses around the primary states more or less.

No matter which state is dominant, the current continues. For example, the model shows sympathetic flight/fight, the middle circle will appear dominant, but the current continues throughout the entire system.

Ventral, sympathetic, dorsal

The three circles

Central to the Polyvagal Current are the three circles, each representing an autonomic primary state.

Ventral

Ventral is the yellow one on the left. This represents your social engagement system. Ventral is the branch driving your potential to connect with others, self, and environment.

Sympathetic

Sympathetic is the red one in the middle. Most people know this branch as fight-or-flight, but that’s only one of its faces. Sympathetic is mobilization: energy, activation, drive. With safety, it shows up as play, excitement, motivation, productivity, and creativity. Without safety, the same activation shows up as anxiety, panic, urgency, and anger.

Dorsal

Dorsal is the blue one on the right, responsible for immobilization. With safety, dorsal shows up as stillness. Stillness is a slow, settled feeling you get when curled up with a book under a blanket or when practicing mindfulness. Without safety, the dorsal autonomic branch shows up as shutdown, experienced as heavy, numb, depressed, and potentially dissociated.

The three circles endlessly spin in the model, showing how each state is always active to some degree. What changes is which one is dominant, and what level of ventral vagal safety is influencing everything.

There’s no top and no bottom in the Polyvagal Current. No beginning and no end. No good or bad, right or wrong.

The three branches are equal peers, in constant relationship with each other. The healthy, regulated current flows fluidly within and without all three branches, using each as necessary, then returns to regulation.

The question, then, is what makes the branches express regulated versus dysregulated. That’s what the slider beneath the Current shows.

Same branch, different face

The Safety Influence slider

To the left of the three circles is a vertical slider labeled Safety Influence. On it are six positions, bottom to top: shutdown, freeze, fight/flight, play, safety, and stillness. These six autonomic states form the primary and mixed states of the Polyvagal Theory.

The slider is essential to showing how safety affects the entire system. The same autonomic branch produces different experiences depending on how much safety your system has access to.

Drag the slider down, and sympathetic shows up as fight-or-flight. Drag it up, and the same branch shows up as play. Drag it further up, and dorsal produces stillness instead of collapsed numbness.

Self-regulation, in this model, isn’t about just climbing back to ventral. It’s about adding safety into the system and how those additions shift the entire system over time.

Once safety is in the system, the states begin to sort themselves out into their regulated forms naturally. The model can also show how stuckness begins to unstuck once enough safety enters the system.

Typically, we ask how to get rid of stuck defense. Like, how do I get rid of shutdown? The Polyvagal Current model reframes the question to one of curiosity: What happens to stuck defense when I add more safety?

The destination isn’t ventral. You’re not supposed to live in ventral. That’s not possible to have 100% ventral all the time. The body achieves the most homeostatic functioning when enough ventral is active in the system. Not total ventral. Enough.

With enough ventral activation, the body can regulate into and out of defensive activation, like sliding the safety influence slider up and down.

The Polyvagal Current model helps reframe the nervous system as something to be curious about, not to judge and fight.

Other models

What makes the Polyvagal Current different

Other models are genuinely useful and stand on their own: the Polyvagal Ladder, the stoplight, the three-color chart with an activation line. (I’ve used Deb Dana’s Polyvagal Ladder extensively for years.) They each show the three autonomic states and indicate sequential shifting between them, and they do that job well.

The Current is built to surface a few additional things alongside them:

  • The mixed states (freeze, play, stillness)
  • The impact of safety on the system as a whole
  • The states as fluid gradients rather than fixed points
  • Stuckness, and how it begins to resolve
A caveat

A general understanding of your state

Like any model, the Polyvagal Current is imperfect.

The base model above represents a very general understanding of how increasing safety can shift an entire autonomic system. But it treats each state as relatively equal. There is simply no way any model can capture a specific person’s version of state shifting.

Someone coming out of shutdown, for example, may go through a brief period of freeze activation. Another may spend more time in freeze. And a third might find freeze negligible. The Current model cannot account for this, nor does it need to.

The model shows each primary and mixed state and suggests what the system may look like very generally. It’s intended to give the viewer a snapshot of their entire system, showing that all three states are still active regardless of the dominant state. It suggests the potential autonomic shifts happening and future potentials as someone increases their safety baseline.

Here is the same Current with each branch on its own control. Set them to where you actually are, rather than to a point on a single line. The primary states are one branch leading; the mixed states are two branches up at once.

Quick answers

FAQ

Is the Polyvagal Current a replacement for the polyvagal ladder?

It’s a different visualization of the same underlying theory. I’ve used the Polyvagal Ladder model extensively for years and it stands on its own.

Is this peer-reviewed?

The underlying neurophysiology (Porges’ polyvagal theory) is peer-reviewed and decades-old. The Current is an original teaching model layered on top of that foundation. The visualization is mine; the science it teaches is established.

Can I use this with my clients?

Yes. The page is free to link to and free to teach from. Attribution appreciated.

Where does Stephen Porges fit in?

Porges’ work is the foundation. The Current is a teaching layer on top of that foundation. It’s a way to show people what the theory looks like in their own body.

How do I actually use this on myself?

That’s the next page: How to read your own nervous system.
